# c-script (Link) — Backend Language with Native End-to-End Type Safety for TypeScript

> c-script is a compiled backend language and toolchain. One `.link` file is the single
> source of truth for your types, your database schema, your RPC endpoints, your auth
> rules and your tests; `linkc build` emits the TypeScript contract, a typed client,
> runtime validators, React hooks, Zod schemas and an OpenAPI 3.1 spec from it. Rename a
> field in the backend and the frontend stops compiling — that is the entire point.

## Names (read this first — they are all the same project)

| Thing | Value |
|---|---|
| Repository | `charlessonamericantrading/c-script-` (the trailing `-` is part of the name) |
| Language name | **c-script** (canonical, decided in PLAN.md "Sobre el nombre") |
| Brand used in the README | **Link** |
| Source file extension | `.link` |
| Compiler / CLI binary | `linkc` |
| Planned npm wrapper | `link-lang` (**not published yet** — `npm i link-lang` fails today; use the [installers](https://github.com/charlessonamericantrading/c-script-/releases) instead) |

## Documentation (absolute URLs — fetch these directly)

- Grammar & full specification (EBNF, bidirectional type checker, c-script→TypeScript mapping table, and the honest limits of every feature): https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charlessonamericantrading/c-script-/master/GRAMMAR.md — large (~190 KB); it has a table of contents at the top, fetch the section you need.
- Engineering plan, architecture and roadmap: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charlessonamericantrading/c-script-/master/PLAN.md
- Instructions for coding agents: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charlessonamericantrading/c-script-/master/AGENTS.md
- Extended LLM reference (type mapping tables, generated-output shapes): https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charlessonamericantrading/c-script-/master/llms-full.txt
- Working reference program (compiles, runs, and is checked by CI on every push): https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charlessonamericantrading/c-script-/master/examples/users.link

## What works today, and what does not

Do not infer capabilities from feature names. This section is the ground truth; if it
disagrees with any prose elsewhere in the repo, this section wins.

Works, verified by running it:

- `linkc build` — emits `contract.d.ts`, `client.ts`, `validators.ts`, `hooks.ts`, `schemas.ts`, `openapi.json`.
- `linkc serve` — real HTTP server, embedded SQLite that persists across restarts, SSE streams.
- `linkc test` — runs `test "..."` blocks against an isolated in-memory database.
- `linkc dev`, `linkc lint`, `linkc doc`, `linkc docker`, `linkc lsp`, `linkc new`, `linkc --help`.
- `linkc fmt` and the TypeScript client emitter for files with multiple `service` blocks.
- Declarative auth: `@authenticated` and `@requires(Role.Admin)`, with session tokens drawn from the OS CSPRNG. `@requires(Role.Admin | Role.Agent)` accepts any of several roles — all from the same enum (mixing two enums in one `@requires` is a parse error) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.49. `linkc serve --session-ttl 7d` (or `LINK_SESSION_TTL`, format `Ns`/`Nm`/`Nh`/`Nd`) makes sessions expire on their own; unset (the default), a session still lives until `destroySession()` or a process restart — see GRAMMAR.md §3.50. `auth.currentRole() -> String?` reads which role authenticated the current request from inside an rpc body (the variant name, e.g. `"Admin"`) — works with no auth annotation at all, `null` if there's no valid session; lets a `Role.Admin | Role.Agent` endpoint behave differently per role instead of just allow/deny — see GRAMMAR.md §3.51.
- External auth: `linkc serve --jwt-secret <secret>` (or `LINK_JWT_SECRET`) verifies an HS256 JWT already issued by an existing backend, alongside (never instead of) Link's own sessions — `@requires`/`@authenticated`/`auth.currentRole()`/`auth.currentUserId()` all work the same regardless of which one authenticated the request. `--jwt-role-claim`/`--jwt-user-id-claim` (or their env vars, default `role`/`sub`) pick which claims carry the role and user id; `sub` accepts a JSON number or a digit string (real OIDC convention). Only HS256 — any other `alg`, including `"none"`, is rejected before checking a signature at all; `exp` is honored if present, no `nbf`/`iss`/`aud`, no RS256/JWKS — see GRAMMAR.md §3.64.
- `crypto.hashPassword` / `verifyPassword` — Argon2id (RFC 9106) with a random per-password salt, PHC format, constant-time verification. Cost is the crate default unless `linkc serve` is started with `--argon2-memory-kib <N>` / `--argon2-iterations <N>` (or `LINK_ARGON2_MEMORY_KIB`/`LINK_ARGON2_ITERATIONS`) — a server-wide setting, not a per-call argument; `verifyPassword` doesn't need it, the PHC hash embeds its own params — see GRAMMAR.md §3.58. `crypto.isLegacyHash(hash: String) -> Bool` reports whether a stored hash is the pre-Argon2id legacy format, for proactive rehashing on login. `crypto.randomToken` and `crypto.uuid` also come from the OS CSPRNG. `crypto.uuid() -> Uuid` returns the native `Uuid` type, not `String` — a separate type validated to the canonical `xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx` form at every JSON boundary, no implicit mixing with `String` (same rule as `Int64` vs `Int`); `.toString()` converts explicitly — see GRAMMAR.md §3.70. `crypto.randomInt(min: Int, max: Int) -> Int` gives a uniform integer in that inclusive range from the same CSPRNG, rejection-sampled against modulo bias (enough for a real OTP, unlike `randomToken`'s hex alphabet); `crypto.timingSafeEqual(a: String, b: String) -> Bool` exposes the constant-time comparison `verifyPassword` already used internally, for comparing a webhook secret or API key without a timing side-channel — see GRAMMAR.md §3.54.
- PostgreSQL as the runtime database: `linkc serve app.link 8787 --db postgres://user:pass@host/db` (or `LINK_DATABASE_URL`). Same program, same generated contract; SQLite stays the default. Opportunistic TLS (pure-rustls, no OpenSSL) via `sslmode` in the URL, and automatic reconnection after a dropped connection (the request that hits the drop still errors; the next one finds a healed connection) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.40. No connection pool (not meaningful — the interpreter is single-threaded, one query in flight at a time) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.36. A preexisting table's autoincrement "id" can be `BIGSERIAL`, `SERIAL`, or a 16-bit `IDENTITY`/`SMALLINT` — all three widths decode correctly, not just 64-bit — see GRAMMAR.md §3.59. Non-destructive auto-migration always adds a new column nullable, even a required one — a pre-existing row with `NULL` there fails that one read with a clean runtime error naming the row and field, never a silent `null` sent to a typed client — see GRAMMAR.md §3.17 (full behavior matrix: new/dropped/renamed column, type change, required↔optional, SQLite and Postgres separately) and §3.68.
- Cross-instance `stream` push via PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY: a `stream` connected to one `linkc serve` process sees a write that came in through a different `linkc serve` process against the same database — works automatically, no config needed. Limits: NOTIFY payload capped at 8000 bytes (Postgres's own limit — an oversized change just doesn't propagate remotely, still publishes locally), best-effort with no retry queue, up to 200ms latency on an idle server, one extra Postgres connection per instance, SQLite doesn't participate — see GRAMMAR.md §3.44.
- `linkc serve --adopt-existing` (or `LINK_ADOPT_EXISTING`): every declared collection assumes its table already exists — never runs `CREATE TABLE` or `ALTER TABLE`, not even the usual non-destructive kind, only read-only checks that each declared column is actually there (SQLite also compares the SQL type; PostgreSQL only checks existence by name, same criterion as the existing `"id"`-type check). A physical column the `.link` doesn't model is ignored, never an error. A missing table, or a missing declared column (even an optional one), fails at connect with a message naming exactly what's missing — never a silent `CREATE`/`ALTER`. All-or-nothing per process (not per collection); doesn't validate `NOT NULL` in SQLite or column-by-column type in PostgreSQL beyond `"id"` — see GRAMMAR.md §3.67.
- Non-JSON responses: `@content_type("text/html; charset=utf-8")` on an rpc returning `String` sends that body verbatim with that header — HTML, XML sitemaps, CSV, plain text. Combines with `@authenticated` / `@requires`.
- `"...".escapeHtml() -> String`: escapes `& < > " '` before interpolating untrusted data into an HTML page — see GRAMMAR.md §3.45. Not automatic; call it where you interpolate.
- `response.setStatus(code: Int) -> Void`: picks the HTTP status for the SUCCESS path of the current rpc (default 200 if never called) — e.g. a branded 404 page for an `@route`+`@content_type("text/html")` rpc that found nothing, or 201 on a plain JSON `create`. Only affects success; an `Err`/panic still always maps to its own status and JSON body, unchanged, even if `setStatus` was called earlier in the same rpc. Runtime-validated to 100–599. Calling it inside a `stream` is a COMPILE ERROR (its status is fixed for the whole SSE connection, so it would be a silent no-op) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.46 and §3.56.
- Friendly URLs: `@route("/blog/:slug")` on an rpc gives it an additional GET-friendly path, alongside (never instead of) the normal `/Service/rpc` address the generated client keeps using. Any number of `:name` segments, in any position (`/blog/:category/:slug`), bound to `String`/`Int` rpc parameters of the same name — by name, not position, so the rpc's param order doesn't have to match the route's. A route with more fixed (literal) segments deterministically wins over a fully dynamic one that would also match the same path — see GRAMMAR.md §3.37 and §3.42. A trailing catch-all segment `:name*` (must be the route's LAST segment) captures zero or more remaining path segments joined by `/`, always as `String` (never `Int`) — `/docs` and `/docs/a/b/c` both match `@route("/docs/:rest*")`, with `rest` `""` and `"a/b/c"` respectively; a more specific literal route always wins over an overlapping catch-all — see GRAMMAR.md §3.57. Any rpc param NOT named in the path is read from the query string by name instead — `String`/`Int` required (400 if missing), `String?`/`Int?` optional (`null` if absent); `body` is still never read (the whole point is a plain-GET URL a crawler can open) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.62.
- `.toString() -> String` on `Int`, `Int64`, `Float` and `Bool` — explicit conversion, never automatic (`'+' ` still requires same-type operands, GRAMMAR.md §3.7). `Bool.toString()` is the first method that exists on `Bool` at all — see GRAMMAR.md §3.55.
- Verifying third-party webhooks: `env.get(name) -> String?` reads a process env var; `request.rawBody() -> String` and `request.header(name) -> String?` expose the exact incoming HTTP body/headers; `crypto.hmacSha256(secret, message) -> String` computes an HMAC-SHA256 hex digest. Together they let an rpc check a webhook's signature before trusting it — see GRAMMAR.md §3.38.
- Per-client rate limiting: `@rate_limit("20/1m")` on an rpc caps it to N requests per time window, per `(client IP, service, rpc)` — 429 on exceeding. Format is `"N/Ns"`, `"N/Nm"` or `"N/Nh"`; combines with any other annotation and runs before the auth gate — see GRAMMAR.md §3.39.
- `@deprecated("usa X en su lugar")` on a struct field OR an rpc/stream — purely informational, zero effect on runtime behavior or on structural subtyping (a struct is still the exact same type whether or not one of its fields carries this). On an rpc it combines freely with any other annotation (`@authenticated`, `@route`, etc.), same mechanism. On a field it is the ONLY annotation a field accepts today — `Field` has no generic annotation list like `RpcDecl` does, so any other name there (`@authenticated`, etc.) is a parse error, not silently ignored. Propagated as a JSDoc `/** @deprecated <reason> */` comment right above the field/method in `contract.d.ts`, and as native `deprecated: true` + `description` (Operation Object / JSON Schema 2020-12 keywords, no `x-*` extension) in `openapi.json` — see GRAMMAR.md §3.71.
- `///` docstrings on an rpc/stream (only — not on `type`/`enum`/a struct field yet), propagated as `description` in `openapi.json` and as a multi-line JSDoc block in `contract.d.ts`. `///` is exactly 3 slashes — `//`/`////` are unaffected, still discarded like any other comment. Purely additive at the lexer level: `///` was already legal in ANY position (same trivia as `//`), so this changes nothing about what compiles — the parser only reads the captured text right above a `rpc`/`stream`, even through an `@annotation` in between. Combines with `@deprecated` on the same rpc into one field/block instead of one overwriting the other — see GRAMMAR.md §3.72.
- Configurable CORS + fixed security headers on `linkc serve`: `--cors-origin <origin>` (repeatable) or `LINK_CORS_ORIGINS` (comma-separated) switches from open `*` to an exact-match allowlist (echoed literal + `Vary: Origin`; a non-matching `Origin` gets no CORS header at all, on every response including `stream` SSE and errors). Every response also carries `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` — see GRAMMAR.md §3.41. No CSP (depends on page content) or HSTS (belongs at the TLS-terminating reverse proxy, not `linkc serve` itself).
- Sending email: `smtp.send(to: String, subject: String, body: String) -> Void`. Connection and sender come from the process environment (`LINK_SMTP_URL`, `LINK_SMTP_FROM`), never from rpc arguments — see GRAMMAR.md §3.43. `smtp.sendToMany(to: String[], subject: String, body: String) -> Void` sends ONE message with one `RCPT TO` per recipient; `smtp.sendHtml(to: String[], subject: String, html: String) -> Void` sends an HTML body (`Content-Type: text/html`) to one or many recipients — see GRAMMAR.md §3.63. All three: no attachments, no cc/bcc, synchronous (blocks the single-threaded server for that request).
- Calling third-party APIs: `http.get(url: String) -> String` / `http.post(url: String, body: String) -> String` (unchanged), plus `http.getWithHeaders(url: String, headers) -> String` / `http.postWithHeaders(url: String, body: String, headers) -> String` for calls that need `Authorization` or any other header. `headers` is `{name: String, value: String}[]` — structural, not a builtin type, so any struct you declare with those two fields works. Response is only the body as `String`; a non-2xx becomes a runtime error (not a value with the status code) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.47. `http.getWithStatus(url: String, headers) -> {status: Int, headers: {name:String,value:String}[], body: String}` / `http.postWithStatus(url: String, body: String, headers) -> same` — two ADDITIONAL methods (the four above are unchanged) that return the status code and response headers as data instead of turning a non-2xx into a runtime error; the return type is structural too, no builtin name — see GRAMMAR.md §3.60.
- `db.<collection>.page(limit: Int, offset: Int) -> T[]`: real pagination — `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` pushed into the actual SQL query on both SQLite and Postgres, not `all().take(n)` (which fetches the whole table first). Same `ORDER BY "id"` as `all()` so pages don't overlap or skip rows. Negative `limit`/`offset` is a runtime error (rejected before reaching SQL, since SQLite and Postgres treat a negative value differently); an `offset` past the end is an empty list, not an error — see GRAMMAR.md §3.48. `db.<collection>.pageAfter(cursor: Int?, limit: Int) -> T[]`: cursor-based alternative for sequential/infinite-scroll pagination — the cursor is the last-seen `id` (`null` for the first page); unlike `OFFSET`, `WHERE "id" > cursor` is stable under concurrent inserts (a row written between two calls never shifts the next page) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.61.

Does NOT work today — do not propose designs that depend on these:

- **Auto HTML escaping.** `"...".escapeHtml()` exists (GRAMMAR.md §3.45, escapes `& < > " '`) but is opt-in — nothing forces you to call it. Pages are still built by concatenating `String`; interpolate untrusted data through `.escapeHtml()` yourself, or it goes into the page as-is.
- **`request.rawBody()` needs a JSON body.** Argument parsing runs before any rpc regardless of its parameter count, so a non-JSON body never reaches the rpc — a JSON webhook payload with extra fields is fine.
- **`@rate_limit` is per-process, in-memory.** No persistence across restarts, no coordination across replicas. The client IP comes from the real TCP connection, never `X-Forwarded-For`.
- **`http.get`/`http.post`/`getWithHeaders`/`postWithHeaders` only return the response body.** No status code or response headers exposed to the program — a 4xx/5xx from the called API is a generic runtime error, not something the rpc can branch on.
- **No `ctx.user` / full caller identity.** `auth.currentRole() -> String?` (GRAMMAR.md §3.51) exposes only the role name — the session never stores a reference to the actual `User` who logged in, only the role tag, same as v0.
- **Native WASM codegen** (`linkc wasm`) is deliberately frozen at integer/boolean scalar functions.
- **No npm package yet.** Prebuilt binaries are on [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/charlessonamericantrading/c-script-/releases); `npm i link-lang` is not published.

## The rules an LLM gets wrong

Every one of these was a real bug in this repository's own documentation. They are the
difference between code that compiles and code that does not.

1. **An enum variant used as a VALUE needs braces**: `Role.Member {}`, not `Role.Member`.
   Inside an annotation it is written without braces: `@requires(Role.Admin)`. Inside a
   `match` pattern, also without braces: `Filter.All => ...`. This single rule causes most
   first-attempt failures.
2. **Closures take no return-type annotation**: `|t: Todo| { !t.completed }`, never
   `|t: Todo| -> Bool { ... }`.
3. **A `T?` still can't be dereferenced via `if`.** `if x != null` type-checks as a boolean
   test but doesn't narrow `x`, so `x.field` inside the branch is still an error — that part
   is deliberate and unchanged. Real narrowing exists through `match` instead:
   `match x { v: T => v.field, null => ... }` binds `v` to the real `T` (GRAMMAR.md §3.69).
   For "give me a default," `x ?? default` is shorter; `x.isSome()`/`x.isNone()` cover "just
   need to know if there's a value" without reading it.
4. **`db.<c>.insert` takes the type without `id`** (`Omit<T, "id">`). Passing a full struct
   with an explicit `id` is accepted, but the value is ignored — the database assigns 1, 2, 3…
5. **`db.<c>.subscribe()` is legal in exactly one place**: as the entire body of
   `stream f() -> T { while true { db.<c>.subscribe() } }`. Anywhere else it is an error.
6. **`Patch<T>` has no literal syntax.** It arrives as an RPC parameter and is passed
   straight to `applyPatch(id, patch)`.
7. **Default parameter values work** (`rpc list(limit: Int = 20)`), including enums — but
   the default obeys rule 1: `rpc list(f: Filter = Filter.All {})`.

8. **`@content_type` only goes on an rpc returning `String`** — never on a `stream`
   (SSE owns its content type), and at most once. Auth annotations stack with it:
   `@requires(Role.Admin) @content_type("text/html")` is valid and is how an admin
   page is written.
9. **`@route`'s path params must be a SUBSET of the rpc's params, matched by name.**
   `@route("/blog/:category/:slug")` requires the rpc to take `category` and `slug`
   somewhere in its params (any order — binding is by name, not position), each
   `String` or `Int`. Any rpc param NOT in the path is read from the query string
   instead (`String`/`Int` required, `String?`/`Int?` optional, `null` if absent) — a
   route with no `:param` at all still works with query-only params, or zero params.
   `body` is still never read on a `@route` GET.
10. **`@rate_limit`'s argument is `"N/window"`, not a sentence.** `"20/1m"` (20 per
    minute), never `"20 per minute"` or `"20/minute"`. Window unit is exactly one of
    `s`/`m`/`h`; the window's number is optional (`"5/m"` means `"5/1m"`) but the
    unit is not.
11. **`sumBy`/`countBy`/`avgBy`/`maxBy`/`minBy`'s selectors must be `|item: T| { item.field }`,
    a bare field access — with the closure braces (rule 2 still applies: no `-> Type`).
    `|o: Order| { o.amount + 1 }` or any other derived expression, method call, or nested
    access is rejected at compile time: it can't be pushed to SQL. Group-by is restricted to
    `String`/`Int`/`Int64`/`Bool`/`enum` fields (no `Float`, no date truncation yet — see
    GRAMMAR.md §3.65); the aggregated field for `sumBy`/`avgBy`/`maxBy`/`minBy` must be
    `Int`/`Int64`/`Float` — an `Int64` result stays `Int64` (string on the wire, §3.30), never
    silently narrowed to `Int`. Neither selector may point at an optional field (`f?: T` or
    `f: T?`).
12. **`Uuid` is not `String` and doesn't mix with it implicitly.** `crypto.uuid()` returns
    `Uuid`, not `String` — `"id: " + crypto.uuid()` is a compile error, same rule as `Int64`
    vs `Int`. Call `.toString()` first to get a plain `String` (then any `String` method works
    on it normally). A `Uuid`-typed field/param rejects anything that isn't the canonical
    `xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx` form (8-4-4-4-12 hex) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.70.
13. **`@deprecated("reason")` on a struct field only accepts THAT annotation, nothing else.**
    `RpcDecl` has a general `Vec<Annotation>` (`@authenticated`/`@route`/`@rate_limit`/etc. all
    combine freely there, `@deprecated` included), but `Field` does not — writing
    `@authenticated legacyPhone: String` on a struct field is a parse error, not something the
    checker rejects later. `@deprecated` is purely informational either way: it never changes
    whether something type-checks, never affects structural subtyping (a struct with a
    deprecated field is still the same type as the identical struct without the annotation),
    and never changes runtime behavior — it only adds a JSDoc `@deprecated` comment to
    `contract.d.ts` and `deprecated: true` + `description` to `openapi.json` — see GRAMMAR.md
    §3.71.

Collection methods, in full: `all()`, `count()`, `find(id) -> T?`, `findWhere(pred) -> T[]`,
`page(limit: Int, offset: Int) -> T[]` (LIMIT/OFFSET pushed to real SQL, not `all().take(n)`
— see GRAMMAR.md §3.48), `insert(Omit<T,"id">) -> T`, `applyPatch(id, patch) -> T`,
`delete(id) -> Bool`, `deleteWhere(pred) -> Int`, `subscribe()` (see rule 5),
`sumBy`/`countBy`/`avgBy`/`maxBy`/`minBy` (`GROUP BY` pushed to real SQL — see rule 11 and
GRAMMAR.md §3.52).

## CLI

```bash
linkc new my-app --template nextjs   # or: vite, minimal
linkc build backend.link src/gen     # TypeScript contract, client, validators, OpenAPI
linkc test backend.link              # run the test blocks
linkc serve backend.link 8787        # HTTP + SQLite + SSE
linkc dev backend.link src/gen 8787  # rebuild and restart on change
linkc introspect postgres://... > main.link  # generate a starting .link from an existing PostgreSQL schema
linkc serve backend.link 8787 --adopt-existing  # never touch DDL; assume every table already exists
```

## Verified example

This program compiles and its test passes. It is re-verified on every CI run by
`compiler/tests/docs_examples.rs`, which is what the `linkc:check` marker below means —
every c-script block in this repository's documentation is compiled by the real binary,
so an example that stops working breaks the build.

<!-- linkc:check -->
```rust
type Todo = {
  id: Int,
  title: String,
  completed: Bool,
  createdAt: Timestamp,
}

// The creation shape: the same fields as Todo without `id` (Omit<Todo, "id">).
type NewTodo = {
  title: String,
  completed: Bool,
  createdAt: Timestamp,
}

enum Filter { All, Pending, Done }

db {
  todos: Todo[],
}

service Todos {
  // Note `Filter.All {}`: an enum variant in expression position needs braces.
  rpc list(filter: Filter = Filter.All {}) -> Todo[] {
    match filter {
      Filter.All => db.todos.all(),
      Filter.Pending => db.todos.findWhere(|t: Todo| { !t.completed }),
      Filter.Done => db.todos.findWhere(|t: Todo| { t.completed }),
    }
  }

  rpc create(title: String) -> Todo {
    db.todos.insert(NewTodo {
      title: title,
      completed: false,
      createdAt: now(),
    })
  }

  // Returns Todo? and hands it to TypeScript as `Todo | null` -- no need to
  // narrow it here since this rpc just passes it through. If you DID need to
  // read a field off it in the backend, `match`/`??`/`.isSome()` narrow a
  // T? for real; `if x != null { x.field }` still doesn't.
  rpc getById(id: Int) -> Todo? {
    db.todos.find(id)
  }

  rpc update(id: Int, patch: Patch<Todo>) -> Todo {
    db.todos.applyPatch(id, patch)
  }

  rpc remove(id: Int) -> Bool {
    db.todos.delete(id)
  }

  // Live push over Server-Sent Events. This exact shape is the only legal
  // position for subscribe().
  stream watch() -> Todo {
    while true {
      db.todos.subscribe()
    }
  }
}

test "a new todo gets an id and starts pending" {
  let created = Todos.create("Learn c-script");
  assert(created.id > 0, "insert assigns the id");
  assert(created.completed == false, "a new todo starts pending");
  assert(Todos.list(Filter.Pending {}).length() == 1, "it shows up under Pending");
}
```

The TypeScript side consumes it with full inference:

```ts
import { createClient } from "./gen/client";

const api = createClient("http://localhost:8787");
const todo = await api.Todos.create("Learn c-script"); // todo: Todo
for await (const t of api.Todos.watch()) console.log(t.title);
```
